name: Gobu
confidence_why: The only source on Gobu itself is Thonner's 1910 traveller's wordlist, whose blanket transcription convention (unmarked words carry the 'Ton' on the penult) and six marked exceptions cannot show whether this Banda language has word stress at all, and the nearest described relatives are tonal and differ from each other on stress (Cotel 1907: mostly penultimate in Togbo; Toqué 1904: initial in Banda-Mbrès), so any stress rule for Gobu would be a guess.
catalog_citation: Thonner, Franz. 1910. Vom Kongo zum Ubangi: Meine zweite Reise in Mittelafrika. Berlin: Dietrich Reimer (Ernst Vohsen). 'Wörterverzeichnisse aus den Sprachen der Eingeborenen', introduction p. 86; Gobu wordlist (Stamm Gobu, Dorf Lele, nächster Posten Mokoange), pp. 91-92. archive.org vomkongozumubang00thon.
catalog_locator: p. 86 (unnumbered page heading the wordlists); Gobu column pp. 91-92
catalog_quote: Die hier und auch sonst in vorliegendem Werke angewandte Schreibart der Wörter aus den Sprachen der Eingeborenen weicht in folgenden Punkten von der deutschen ab. ... Lange Selbstlaute sind mit einem Dehnungszeichen versehen. Wo kein Betonungszeichen angegeben ist, ruht der Ton auf der vorletzten Silbe. Diese Schreibart stimmt mit der in der belgischen Kongokolonie üblichen überein; jedoch unterdrückt letztere das im Anlaut mancher Wörter vor einem Mitlaute stehende M und N (so Bomu statt Mbomu, Dobo statt Ndobo, Gali statt Ngali), was ich nicht für gerechtfertigt halte. Sämtliche in nachstehendem Verzeichnis aufgeführten Wörter, mit Ausnahme der der Bangala-Sprache, welche die allgemeine Verkehrssprache am Kongo bildet, habe ich unmittelbar von den Eingeborenen in den betreffenden Dörfern erfragt. [p. 86] ... Stamm Gobu / Dorf Lele / Nächst. Posten Mokoange: Ein obali, Zwei bisi, Drei vota, Vier vona, Fünf mitú, Sechs siti, Sieben mobisi, Acht mavuta, Neun mavona, Zehn plafu, Auge la, Nase o, Ohr tu, Mund ma, Zunge tima, Zahn isi, Haar li, Hals ngi, Arm liboko, Finger yátina, Brust lesu, Bauch selingi, Bein ku, Mann sokoli, Frau yilu, Kind bemulenge, Häuptling mukundji, Dorf kódroma, Weg wa, Haus plida [p. 91]; Dach yeyó, Kahn ngo, Ruder kai, Speer du, Brennholz wo, Wasser ngu, Salz imbri, Banane gwa, Huhn ngatu, Ziege mangwa. 1) látebi wahrscheinlich = dein Auge. 2) ótibi wahrscheinlich = deine Nase. [p. 92]

new_statements.translation: Long vowels are given a length mark. Where no stress mark is given, the stress (Ton) rests on the penultimate syllable. This spelling agrees with the one customary in the Belgian Congo colony [...] All the words listed in the following list, except those of the Bangala language [...], I asked for directly from the natives in the villages concerned.
new_statements.citation: Thonner, Franz. 1910. Vom Kongo zum Ubangi: Meine zweite Reise in Mittelafrika. Berlin: Dietrich Reimer (Ernst Vohsen). 'Wörterverzeichnisse aus den Sprachen der Eingeborenen', p. 86; Gobu wordlist pp. 91-92.
new_statements.locator: p. 86 (introduction to the wordlists; unnumbered page between pp. 85 and 87, PDF page 102); Gobu column pp. 91-92 (PDF pages 107-108)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened via the saved renders and scanned. pages/unnumbered printed p. 86, PDF page 102, heading 'Wörterverzeichnisse aus den Sprachen der Eingeborenen') carries the quoted text word for word: 'Lange Selbstlaute sind mit einem Dehnungszeichen versehen. Wo kein Betonungszeichen angegeben ist, ruht der Ton auf der vorletzten Silbe. Diese Schreibart stimmt mit der in der belgischen Kongokolonie üblichen überein; jedoch unterdrückt letztere das im Anlaut mancher Wörter.. M und N..' and, next paragraph, 'Sämtliche in nachstehendem Verzeichnis aufgeführten Wörter, mit Ausnahme der der Bangala-Sprache, welche die allgemeine Verkehrssprache am Kongo bildet, habe ich unmittelbar von den Eingeborenen…
new_statements.rule_in_words: This is only a transcription convention covering every wordlist in the book (Bangala, Sango, Banziri, Gobu, Banza, Bwaka..): unmarked words are to be read with penultimate 'Ton', marked words otherwise. In the Gobu column (village Lele near Mokoange on the Ubangi) most items are unmarked, while mitú 'five' (final), yátina 'finger' and kódroma 'village' (initial/antepenult) carry an acute. It is a traveller-botanist's 1910 elicitation, not a phonological description; Banda varieties are tonal (three level tones per Cotel 1907 on Togbo and later work on Linda/Tangbago/Mono), so Thonner's 'Ton' very likely records pitch prominence rather than a stress system. It cannot be taken as a statement that Gobu has fixed penultimate word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Only implicitly: the Gobu items marked with an acute on a non-penultimate syllable (mitú, yátina, kódroma); Thonner also notes speakers often reduplicate or add possessive suffixes to elicited words (tutu for tu 'spear').
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms in a 60-item comparative wordlist; the convention is stated once for the whole book, not for Gobu specifically. Two open old Banda grammars for OTHER varieties disagree with each other (Cotel 1907, Togbo [tor], p. XI: mostly penultimate accent plus three tones; Toqué 1904, Banda-Mbrès [bqk], pp. 63-64: initial accent in 2-3-syllable words, 1st and 3rd in 4-syllable words), which further shows that pre-phonemic 'accent' statements on Banda are unreliable proxies for Gobu.
new_statements.identity_note: Gobu [gox] / gobu1238 is a Central Banda variety of the Ubangi (Mobayi-Mbongo area, DRC, and adjacent CAR); Thonner's 1910 wordlist is from the Gobu (Ngobu) village Lele near Mokoange on the Ubangi, i.e. the DRC Gobu. Glottolog's sole descriptive reference, Santandrea 1965, treats 'Gābu' of western Bahr el Ghazal (Sudan), which Glottolog equates with [gox]; that equation is unverified here. The two open Banda grammars examined describe other varieties: Cotel 1907 = Togbo (Banda-Togbo-Vara [tor], togb1240 area) and Toqué 1904 = Banda-Mbrès [bqk]; they are not Gobu and contradict each other on accent placement.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record (Thonner 1910) is 'undetermined': Thonner's 'Wo kein Betonungszeichen angegeben ist, ruht der Ton auf der vorletzten Silbe' is a transcription convention of a 1910 travel wordlist, read held by the project as unclear. Cloarec-Heiss 1978 (snippets) types gubü/Banda as a three-register tone language with open syllables and says nothing about stress or accent: compatible with 'undetermined' for stress and adds the prosodic type (tonal, 3 levels). It neither confirms nor denies a penultimate prominence; no contradiction can be asserted from snippets.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement covering all Banda lects sampled, gubü of Kouango (= Gobu) among them: open (CV) syllable structure and three level tones (three registers). The volume's full-text index returns no occurrence of accent, accentué(e), intensité, proéminence, hauteur or tonique anywhere in the book, so the study types the language as tonal and makes no statement about word stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing (no stress statement of any kind in the indexed text)
new_statements.exceptions: none seen in the snippets; the statement is explicitly for 'toutes les langues de ce groupe'. gubü is sampled with only 79 lexical items and is noted as a 'dialecte ngobou' that 'pourrait éventuellement se rattacher' to another group (classification remark, not prosodic).
new_statements.identity_note: Cloarec-Heiss 1978 samples 'gubü (de Kouango)', labelled 'dialecte ngobou', with 79 lexical items, alongside lindä (Ippy), yäkpà (Kouango), làngbàsi (Kouango), ngbügù (Mobaye), gbi (Grimari), mbanza (Mongoumba), mbänjä (Bujala, Zaire), ngündù (Bianga), ngbündü (Mongoumba), kpäguà (Kouango). gubü of Kouango (CAR) = Glottolog gobu1238 Gobu/Gubu (alt. Gabou, Gabu). The prosodic sentence is stated for 'toutes les langues de ce groupe' (the Banda group), not for gubü individually. Thonner's 1910 Gobu list is from Dorf Lele near Mokoange (Ubangi, then Belgian Congo), i.e. the DR Congo side of the same lect cluster.

sources.note: NOT Gobu (Glottolog/hh.bib assign it to Togbo = Banda-Togbo-Vara [tor]): 'L'accent est le plus souvent sur l'avant-dernière syllabe'; lists exceptional final-stress words (kradzèy', ubùn'..) and a small number of trisyllables with antepenult stress (bá'mara, ku'sara..); then 'Intonation': three tones (élevé, moyen, bas) distinguishing homonyms (kān'ga shoulder/bottle/slave).

sources.citation: Toqué, Georges. 1904. Essai sur le peuple et la langue banda (Région du Tchad). Paris: J. André. pp. 63-64 ('Accent tonique').
sources.note: NOT Gobu (hh.bib assigns it to Banda-Mbrès [bqk]: Ndi, Morouba, Ngao, Sabanga, Tambaggo): 'Règle I. Dans les mots de deux ou trois syllabes, l'accent tonique se place sur la première'; 'Règle II. Dans les mots de quatre syllabes, l'accent tonique se place sur la première et la troisième syllabe'; Règle III penult is weak; Règle IV compounds keep each member's accent; absence of accent can change meaning (bánga 'rubber' vs banga 'cheek').
